services.name: Adobe
services.summary: Adobe says it doesn't train its Firefly generative AI on your files, but by default it may analyse content you store in Creative Cloud or Document Cloud to improve its products. You can turn this off.

training.details: For personal accounts, Adobe's “content analysis” setting lets Adobe analyse content that is processed or stored on its servers when you use Creative Cloud and Document Cloud apps (for example with machine-learning techniques) to improve its products and services. It is on by default for personal accounts; minors and business, team or school accounts are automatically opted out. Adobe says it does not analyse your content to train generative AI models unless you submit it to the Adobe Stock marketplace, and that Firefly models are trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and on public-domain material. Turning content analysis off does not cover programs where you actively submit content to Adobe, or content analysed while you are not signed in. Adobe says it aggregates content before analysis and uses safeguards for human review.

services.name: Amazon Alexa
services.summary: Amazon uses your Alexa and Alexa+ interactions, including voice recordings, transcripts and typed requests, to train its models, with a small sample reviewed by people. You can limit the use of voice recordings.

training.details: Amazon says it uses Alexa interactions (voice recordings, text transcripts, typed requests and other interactions) to improve Alexa and to train its machine-learning models, including supervised learning in which people review a very small sample of requests. It may also use Alexa interactions to improve other Amazon services, such as shopping search. The “Help improve Alexa” settings (use of voice recordings, and use of messages to improve transcriptions) are on by default. Turning them off limits how your voice recordings are used to develop features and be reviewed, but Amazon still keeps text transcripts and typed requests to improve its services. In March 2025 Amazon removed the on-device “Do Not Send Voice Recordings” option from the few Echo models that had it, so requests are processed in Amazon's cloud. Amazon says deleting your data does not remove it from systems already trained on it.

regionNotes.EU: The same Alexa Privacy settings apply. You can also object to processing under GDPR through the privacy contact listed in your country's Amazon privacy notice.
regionNotes.UK: You can object to processing under UK GDPR through Amazon's EU privacy team (eu-privacy@amazon.co.uk).

Under Help improve Alexa, turn off the use of voice recordings.

optOuts.effect: Your future voice recordings are no longer used to develop new features or manually reviewed. Amazon may still use text transcripts and other interaction data to improve its services, and past training is not undone.

optOuts.title: Choose not to save Alexa voice recordings
optOuts.description: Deletes recordings after each request is processed, which limits what can be reused later.
steps: In Alexa Privacy, open Manage Your Alexa Data.
In the voice recordings section, choose not to save recordings.
Confirm. Existing recordings are deleted.
optOuts.effect: Voice recordings are deleted after Alexa processes each request, and existing ones are erased. Text transcripts and typed requests are still kept for 30 days and may be used to improve Amazon's services. Voice ID stops working.

ChatGPT Business (formerly Team), Enterprise, Edu and API data is not used for training by default. services.name: Facebook
services.summary: Meta trains its AI on public Facebook posts, comments and photos from adults, and on your chats with Meta AI. The EU, UK, Switzerland and Brazil have an objection form; the US and most other countries have no opt-out.

training.details: Meta trains its generative AI models (Llama and the models behind Meta AI) on content adults share publicly on Facebook, such as public posts, comments, and photos with their captions, and on your interactions with Meta AI. Meta says it only uses public content and does not train on private messages with friends and family unless you or someone in the chat shares them with Meta AI. Photos or posts of you that other people share publicly can still be used even if you object. Since 16 December 2025, outside the EU, UK and South Korea, Meta also uses your Meta AI chats to personalise the content and ads you see, with no opt-out.

regionNotes.AU: No opt-out. Meta confirmed to an Australian Senate inquiry in 2024 that it trains on public posts from Australian adults. Meta says it only trains on public content, so you can set future posts to Friends (Settings › Audience and visibility › Posts), use “Limit who can see past posts”, or delete public posts. Avoid Meta AI if you don’t want your chats used.
regionNotes.BR: After Brazil’s data regulator (ANPD) paused Meta’s plans in 2024, Meta resumed with notices and an objection form for Brazilian users.
regionNotes.CH: Swiss users were included from 27 May 2025 and can object with the same form (choose Switzerland as your country).
regionNotes.EU: Since 27 May 2025 Meta has trained on public Facebook content from adults in the EU/EEA, relying on “legitimate interests”. You can object at any time with Meta’s form; an objection only covers future training. Public content from under-18s in the EU is not used.
regionNotes.OTHER: Outside the EU/EEA, UK, Switzerland and Brazil, Meta offers no opt-out in most countries, including Canada, India and Japan. Meta says it only trains on public content, so you can set future posts to Friends (Settings › Audience and visibility › Posts), use “Limit who can see past posts”, or delete public posts. Avoid Meta AI if you don’t want your chats used.
regionNotes.UK: Meta began training on UK adults’ public posts in late 2024 after changes agreed with the ICO. UK users can object with the same form, which only covers future training.
regionNotes.US: No opt-out. Meta has used public posts from US adults to train its AI since at least 2023. Meta says it only trains on public content, so you can set future posts to Friends (Settings › Audience and visibility › Posts), use “Limit who can see past posts”, or delete public posts. Avoid Meta AI if you don’t want your chats used.

optOuts.title: Object to Meta using your Facebook data for AI

Choose your country and enter the email address on your account. Add a short reason if the form asks for one.

training.details: Figma added a team-level “content training” setting that took effect on 15 August 2024. When it is on, Figma may use customer content (file content created in or uploaded to Figma, such as layer names and properties, text and images, comments and annotations) to train its AI models. Starter and Professional plans are opted in by default; Organization and Enterprise plans are opted out by default. training.details: With Keep Activity on (called Gemini Apps Activity until 2025, and on by default if you are 18 or over), Google saves your Gemini chats to your account (auto-deleted after 18 months unless you change it) and uses them, plus a sample of your uploads since 2 September 2025, to improve Google services, including its AI models. With Keep Activity off, or in a Temporary Chat, chats are still kept for up to 72 hours to reply to you and keep the service safe, but Google says they are not used to improve its AI models unless you send feedback. Audio, Gemini Live video and screen shares are only used if you tick a separate box, which is off by default. Work and school (Google Workspace) accounts are not used to train models outside your organisation, and only an administrator can change their Keep Activity setting.

services.name: Instagram
services.summary: Meta trains its AI on public Instagram posts, captions and comments from adults, and on your chats with Meta AI. The EU, UK, Switzerland and Brazil have an objection form; the US and most other countries have no opt-out.

training.details: Meta trains its generative AI models on content adults share publicly on Instagram, such as public posts, photos and their captions, and comments, and on your interactions with Meta AI (including AI chats in Instagram Direct). Meta says it only uses public content, so posts from private accounts are not used, and it does not train on private messages with friends unless someone shares them with Meta AI. Teen Accounts are private by default. Public posts of you by other people can still be used even if you object. Since 16 December 2025, outside the EU, UK and South Korea, your Meta AI chats also shape the content and ads you see, with no opt-out.

regionNotes.AU: No opt-out. Meta confirmed to an Australian Senate inquiry in 2024 that it trains on public posts from Australian adults. Meta says it doesn’t train on private accounts, so you can turn on Private account (Settings and activity › Account privacy) or delete public posts. Avoid Meta AI if you don’t want your chats used.
regionNotes.BR: After Brazil’s data regulator (ANPD) paused Meta’s plans in 2024, Meta resumed with notices and an objection form for Brazilian users.
regionNotes.CH: Swiss users were included from 27 May 2025 and can object with the same form (choose Switzerland as your country).
regionNotes.EU: Since 27 May 2025 Meta has trained on public Instagram content from adults in the EU/EEA, relying on “legitimate interests”. You can object at any time with Meta’s form; an objection only covers future training. Public content from under-18s in the EU is not used.
regionNotes.OTHER: Outside the EU/EEA, UK, Switzerland and Brazil, Meta offers no opt-out in most countries, including Canada, India and Japan. Meta says it doesn’t train on private accounts, so you can turn on Private account (Settings and activity › Account privacy) or delete public posts. Avoid Meta AI if you don’t want your chats used.
regionNotes.UK: Meta began training on UK adults’ public posts in late 2024 after changes agreed with the ICO. UK users can object with the same form, which only covers future training.
regionNotes.US: No opt-out. Meta has used public posts from US adults to train its AI since at least 2023. Meta says it doesn’t train on private accounts, so you can turn on Private account (Settings and activity › Account privacy) or delete public posts. Avoid Meta AI if you don’t want your chats used.

optOuts.title: Object to Meta using your Instagram data for AI
optOuts.description: Meta’s “right to object” form for AI at Meta. One objection should cover accounts linked in the same Accounts Center; if in doubt, also submit the Facebook form.

services.name: Microsoft Copilot
services.summary: Microsoft says chats in the updated Copilot app (from August 2026) are not used to train its foundation models. The older app could train on your text and voice chats unless you switched that off.

training.details: Microsoft is moving personal accounts to an updated Microsoft Copilot app, available since 18 August 2026. For that app, Microsoft states that your prompts, responses and file contents are not used to train foundation models, and its privacy settings no longer include a training switch. Optional feedback may still be used to improve Copilot. In the previous consumer app, Microsoft could use your de-identified text and voice conversations to train its generative AI models by default, with switches to opt out. That did not apply to users under 18, signed-out users, or users in the EEA and several other countries. Work or school (Entra ID) accounts and Copilot inside Microsoft 365 Personal and Family apps are not used for training. Microsoft's general privacy statement still says it may use data to develop and train AI models, so if you still use the older app, check its Privacy settings.

regionNotes.BR: Copilot conversations from Brazil are excluded from model training (as are China excluding Hong Kong, Israel, Nigeria, South Korea and Vietnam).
regionNotes.EU: Microsoft says it does not train its models on consumer Copilot data from the European Economic Area, so the training switches are not shown there.
regionNotes.UK: Microsoft's list of excluded places does not name the UK. If the older app shows you the training switches, turn them off.

optOuts.title: Turn off training on your conversations (older Copilot app)
optOuts.description: Only in the previous version of the Copilot app. The updated app (from August 2026) has no training switch, because Microsoft says it doesn't train foundation models on those chats.
steps: Open Copilot and sign in with your Microsoft account.
Select your profile icon, then your profile name, then Privacy. In the Windows or Mac app: profile icon → Settings → Privacy. In the mobile app: menu → profile icon → Account → Privacy.
Turn off “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations” (some versions call them “Model training on text” and “Model training on voice”).
If you don't see these switches, you are on the updated app or in a place where training is already off.
optOuts.effect: Excludes your future conversations from training Microsoft's AI models. It does not stop use for safety, general product improvement or advertising, and does not remove past data.

services.name: Reddit
services.summary: Reddit licenses public posts and comments to AI companies such as Google and OpenAI for training. There is no opt-out, but licensees must stop using content you delete.

training.details: Reddit licenses public content (posts, comments and media in public communities) to AI companies, including Google (from 2024) and OpenAI, which can use it to train and power their models; Reddit also uses content for its own AI features. Private messages, chats and content in private communities are not licensed. Reddit requires licensees to stop using or displaying content once you delete it, but it cannot control copies others have scraped, and it is unclear whether deleted content is removed from models already trained. Reddit’s privacy policy effective 1 July 2026 also lists “LLM providers” that help summarise public content for search results on Reddit.

regionNotes.EU: No dedicated opt-out. Under GDPR you can ask Reddit to erase your data or object to processing by emailing its privacy team; deleting your content is still the most effective step.

EU/UK users can also email an objection or erasure request to redditdatarequests@reddit.com.
optOuts.effect: Deletion is the only lever: licensees must stop using deleted content from then on, but data already used for training is not removed.

services.name: Slack
services.summary: Slack doesn't train generative AI on your messages, but by default uses workspace data to train its other machine-learning models (search, emoji and channel suggestions). Only a workspace owner can opt out, by email.

training.details: Slack says it does not develop generative AI models using customer data and will not use customer data to train generative AI models without the customer's affirmative opt-in. Its AI features use third-party large language models hosted inside Slack's own infrastructure, which do not retain or learn from your data. Separately, Slack analyses customer data (such as messages, content and files) together with usage information to train “global” non-generative machine-learning models for features like channel and emoji recommendations, search ranking and autocomplete. Slack says these models use de-identified, aggregate data and are built so they cannot learn, memorise or reproduce customer data. Workspaces are included unless they opt out. Because Slack processes messages on behalf of the organisation that owns the workspace, only that organisation's owners can opt out; individual members cannot.

regionNotes.EU: For workspaces set up outside the US and Canada, Slack Technologies Limited (Dublin) processes workspace content on behalf of the organisation that owns the workspace, so requests about that content usually go through your organisation's admins.
regionNotes.UK: Slack Technologies Limited (Dublin) processes workspace content on behalf of the organisation that owns the workspace, so requests about that content usually go through your organisation's admins.

optOuts.title: Ask your workspace owner to email Slack a global model opt-out
optOuts.description: Slack only accepts this request from an Org Owner, Workspace Owner or Primary Owner, sent to feedback@slack.com (not privacy@slack.com). Regular members need to ask their admin.
steps: If you are a regular member, ask your Workspace Owner, Primary Owner or Org Owner to send this request; members can't opt out themselves.
The owner emails feedback@slack.com.
Subject line: “Slack global model opt-out request”.
Include the workspace or org URL (for example yourteam.slack.com).
Slack replies once the opt-out has been completed.
optOuts.effect: Stops that workspace's data helping to train Slack's global (non-generative) machine-learning models; it is then only used to improve the experience in your own workspace. Features keep working. It does not affect data already used.

services.name: Snapchat
services.summary: Snap can train its generative AI on your public Snaps (Spotlight, public Stories, Snap Map) and uses My AI chats to improve its products. Public-content use is on by default and can be switched off.

training.details: Snap may use images, video, audio and text you post publicly on Snapchat, such as Spotlight, public Stories and Snap Map, to develop, train and improve its generative AI models. An in-app Generative AI setting (“Allow use of public content”) is on by default and stops this going forward. Separately, content you share with My AI is kept until you delete it and is used to improve Snap’s products, including the models behind My AI, and to personalise ads; there is no setting to stop that, but you can clear your My AI data (deletion can take up to 30 days). Private Snaps and chats with friends are not part of the public-content training, but you may still appear in other people’s public posts.

regionNotes.EU: You can also use your GDPR right to object by contacting Snap’s Data Protection Officer.
regionNotes.UK: You can also use your UK GDPR right to object by contacting Snap’s Data Protection Officer.

optOuts.title: Turn off “Allow use of public content” for generative AI
optOuts.description: An in-app setting with no web version, so NoTrain can only guide you. The link opens Snap’s help page. It does not cover My AI chats.
steps: Open Snapchat, tap your profile icon, then the gear icon to open Settings.
Scroll to Privacy Controls and open the Generative AI settings.
Turn off “Allow use of public content”.
Optional: to delete past My AI chats, use “Clear My AI Data” in Settings.
optOuts.effect: Snap stops using your public content to train its generative AI from now on. Past training isn’t undone, My AI chats are still used, and you may still appear in others’ public posts.

services.name: Stack Overflow
services.summary: Questions, answers and comments you post publicly on Stack Overflow are licensed to AI companies such as OpenAI and Google for model training. There is no opt-out, and deleting posts is restricted.

training.details: Content you contribute publicly to Stack Overflow and other Stack Exchange sites is published under a Creative Commons licence (CC BY-SA). Since 2024 Stack Overflow has also licensed this content to AI developers through its OverflowAPI product, with partners including Google (announced February 2024) and OpenAI (May 2024), who use it to train and improve their models. There is no setting to exclude your posts. Site rules limit deleting or defacing posts that others have answered or voted on, and moderators can restore them. Deleting your account removes your profile, but your public posts generally stay on the site without your name.

regionNotes.EU: You can send an objection or erasure request to privacy@stackoverflow.com under GDPR, but public posts are published under CC BY-SA and the outcome for AI licensing is uncertain.
regionNotes.UK: You can send an objection or erasure request to privacy@stackoverflow.com under UK GDPR, but public posts are published under CC BY-SA and the outcome for AI licensing is uncertain.

optOuts.title: No opt-out: public posts are licensed for AI training
optOuts.description: Stack Overflow offers no setting to keep your public contributions out of AI data licensing.
steps: There is no setting to stop your public posts being licensed for AI training.
Avoid posting content you don't want reused; posts are licensed CC BY-SA.
In the EU or UK you can still send an objection letter to privacy@stackoverflow.com, though it may not change how public posts are licensed.
optOuts.effect: Nothing stops licensing of content you have already posted publicly. An objection letter creates a record but may not change the outcome.

services.name: Substack
services.summary: Public Substack posts are open to AI crawlers unless the writer turns on “Block AI training” for the publication. Only publication owners can change it; readers and commenters can't.

training.details: Each Substack publication has a “Block AI training” setting that is off by default. When it is on, Substack adds rules to the publication's robots.txt asking AI crawlers (for example OpenAI's GPTBot, Anthropic's ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended) not to collect the publication's content. It is only a request: crawlers that ignore robots.txt are not stopped, and it does not remove content already collected. The setting applies per publication and can only be changed by the publication's owner or admins, so readers, commenters and guest contributors cannot opt out on their own. We did not find a Substack statement about training its own AI models on publications, so this entry focuses on third-party AI training.

optOuts.title: Turn on “Block AI training” for your publication
optOuts.description: A publication-level setting for writers. Its settings page lives on your own publication address (yourname.substack.com/publish/settings).
steps: Sign in to Substack.
Open your publication's dashboard and go to Settings (address: yourname.substack.com/publish/settings).
Turn on “Block AI training”.
Repeat for each publication you run.
optOuts.effect: Adds robots.txt rules asking AI crawlers not to use your publication for training. Crawlers that ignore robots.txt are not blocked, content already collected is not removed, and your posts may show up less in AI tools.

services.name: Threads
services.summary: Meta can train its AI on public Threads posts from adults and on your chats with Meta AI. Threads has no opt-out of its own; in the EU, UK, Switzerland and Brazil you object through Meta’s Instagram form.

training.details: A Threads profile is part of your Instagram account and is covered by Meta’s Privacy Policy and the Threads Supplemental Privacy Policy. Public Threads posts and replies from adults are public content on Meta’s products, which Meta uses to train its generative AI, and by using Threads you agree that your interactions with AIs are used to improve AI at Meta. Meta has not published a Threads-specific objection form or said explicitly whether its Instagram objection covers Threads; objections are applied to accounts in the same Accounts Center, so submitting the Instagram form is the best available route. Posts from a private Threads profile are not public.

regionNotes.BR: Brazilian users can object through Meta’s Instagram or Facebook form.
regionNotes.CH: Swiss users can object through the Instagram form (choose Switzerland as your country).
regionNotes.EU: Meta has trained on public content from EU/EEA adults since 27 May 2025. Object through the Instagram form linked to your Threads profile; the objection only covers future training.
regionNotes.OTHER: Outside the EU/EEA, UK, Switzerland and Brazil, Meta offers no opt-out in most countries. You can make your Threads profile private (Settings › Privacy › Private profile) or delete public posts. Avoid Meta AI if you don’t want your chats used.
regionNotes.UK: UK users can object through the Instagram form linked to their Threads profile.
regionNotes.US: No opt-out. You can make your Threads profile private (Settings › Privacy › Private profile) or delete public posts. Avoid Meta AI if you don’t want your chats used.

optOuts.title: Object via Meta’s Instagram form (covers linked accounts)
optOuts.description: There is no Threads-only form. Submit Meta’s Instagram objection while signed in to the Instagram account behind your Threads profile.
steps: Sign in to Instagram with the account your Threads profile uses.
Open the objection form, choose your country and enter the email address on your account.
Add a short reason if the form asks for one, then submit.
Keep the confirmation email Meta sends you.
optOuts.effect: Once accepted, Meta should stop using your public content and Meta AI chats for future training across linked accounts. Meta hasn’t confirmed Threads is covered, and past training is not undone.

services.name: TikTok
services.summary: TikTok’s privacy policy lets it use your videos, comments and activity to train its machine-learning and AI systems. There’s no setting to opt out; in the EU, UK and Switzerland you can object in writing.

training.details: TikTok’s privacy policies say it uses the information it collects, including content you post and how you use the app, to develop and improve its platform, including by training its machine learning models and algorithms. That powers recommendations, moderation and TikTok’s generative AI features. TikTok offers no setting to stop this. It publishes little detail on how much public content trains its generative models specifically, so treat this entry as a summary of its privacy policy.

regionNotes.EU: You can object under GDPR Article 21 to processing based on legitimate interests using TikTok’s privacy request form; TikTok must stop unless it shows compelling grounds.
regionNotes.OTHER: No opt-out outside the EU/EEA, UK and Switzerland. A private account (Settings and privacy › Privacy › Private account) limits who sees your videos, and you can delete content, but neither stops TikTok using what you post for its own models.
regionNotes.UK: You can object under UK GDPR Article 21 using TikTok’s privacy request form.
regionNotes.US: Covered by TikTok’s US privacy policy. No opt-out. A private account (Settings and privacy › Privacy › Private account) limits who sees your videos, and you can delete content, but neither stops TikTok using what you post for its own models.

optOuts.title: Object to AI training via TikTok’s privacy request form
optOuts.description: A formal objection for people covered by GDPR, UK GDPR or the Swiss FADP.
steps: Open TikTok’s privacy request form and sign in if asked.
Choose the option for exercising a data protection right.
State that you object under Article 21 GDPR to TikTok using your content and activity to train machine learning and AI models.
Submit and keep the confirmation.
optOuts.effect: TikTok must assess your objection and stop unless it has compelling grounds. It only affects future processing.

services.name: Tumblr
services.summary: Tumblr shares public blog content with partners, including AI companies, unless you turn on “Prevent third-party sharing” for each blog. It’s off by default unless you already discourage search engines.

training.details: In February 2024 Tumblr’s owner Automattic confirmed it shares public content with a network of licensed content and research partners, including companies that train AI models (reported to include OpenAI and Midjourney). The “Prevent third-party sharing” switch in each blog’s Visibility settings keeps that blog out; it is off by default, but is switched on automatically if you already chose to discourage external search engines. Automattic said it would tell partners about opt-outs and ask them to delete opted-out content from past and future training, which can’t be guaranteed. Reporting in 2024 raised questions about content compiled before the switch existed.

optOuts.title: Turn on “Prevent third-party sharing” for each blog
optOuts.description: A per-blog switch. Turning it ON is what opts you out. NoTrain’s automation handles your first listed blog; repeat for side blogs.
steps: Sign in to Tumblr on the web and open Settings.
Pick a blog from the Blogs list.
Under Visibility, turn on “Prevent third-party sharing for [blog name]”.
Repeat for every blog you run, including side blogs. In the app: Account › gear icon › choose the blog › Visibility.
optOuts.effect: Stops that blog’s content being shared with Tumblr’s licensed partners, including AI companies, from now on. Automattic says it asks partners to delete opted-out content, but past sharing can’t be fully undone.

services.name: WordPress.com
services.summary: Automattic may share public WordPress.com site content with licensed partners, including companies that train AI models, unless you tick “Prevent third-party sharing” for each of your sites.

training.details: Automattic, which runs WordPress.com, shares content from public WordPress.com sites with “our licensed network of content and research partners, including those that train AI models”. Each site has a “Prevent third-party sharing” option in its visibility settings; public sites are shared unless the owner ticks it. Sites set to discourage search engines are treated as opted out automatically, and the option only appears for public sites. The setting is per site, so it has to be set on every public site you own. It only covers sharing by Automattic; it cannot stop other AI crawlers that ignore your site's preferences.

optOuts.title: Tick “Prevent third-party sharing” for each site
optOuts.description: A per-site checkbox in the site's visibility (privacy) settings. When ticked, the site is opted out.

Click Save.
Repeat for every public site you own.
optOuts.effect: Automattic stops sharing that site's content with its licensed content and research partners, including AI companies, from now on. Content shared earlier is not recalled.

services.name: X (Twitter)
services.summary: X shares your public posts and Grok chats with xAI to train Grok, and may let other companies train AI on them. It’s on by default; a checkbox in X’s privacy settings turns it off.

training.details: X shares data such as your public profile, public posts, engagement and your interactions with Grok with its affiliate xAI, which uses it to train and fine-tune Grok. X’s privacy policy also lets “third-party collaborators” use your data to train their own AI models unless you opt out. Both are controlled by one checkbox under Settings and privacy › Privacy and safety › Grok & Third-party Collaborators, which is ticked by default. X’s terms (updated 15 January 2026) grant X a broad licence to use your content, including Grok prompts and outputs, for training AI. Posts from protected accounts are reported not to be used. The standalone Grok app at grok.com has its own training setting (see the separate Grok entry).

regionNotes.EU: After action by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission, X agreed in 2024 not to use EU/EEA users’ public posts collected between 7 May and 1 August 2024 to train Grok. In April 2025 the DPC opened a formal inquiry into Grok training on EU posts. The checkbox works in the EU, and you can also object under GDPR Article 21 through X’s privacy form.
regionNotes.UK: You can also object under UK GDPR Article 21 through X’s privacy form.

services.name: YouTube
services.summary: Google trains its own AI models on YouTube videos, and creators can’t opt out of that. Whether other AI companies may train on your videos is a creator setting that stays off unless you turn it on.

training.details: YouTube’s terms let Google use content uploaded to YouTube to improve its products, including through machine learning and AI. Google has confirmed it trains models such as Gemini and Veo on a subset of YouTube videos, under its agreements with creators; there is no opt-out from Google’s own use. Since December 2024, creators can choose in YouTube Studio whether specific third-party AI companies may train on their videos. This “Third-party training” setting is off by default, and YouTube says unauthorised scraping still breaks its terms. Viewers’ watch and search history is used for recommendations and can be paused or deleted in your Google Account.

regionNotes.EU: No dedicated opt-out from Google’s training. You can contact Google’s privacy team or DPO to object under GDPR Article 21.

optOuts.title: No opt-out from Google training on YouTube videos
optOuts.description: Nothing stops Google using uploaded videos for its own AI. Creators can only control third-party companies, and that is off unless they turn it on.
steps: Creators: sign in to YouTube Studio on a computer and click Settings.
Open Channel › Advanced settings and check “Third-party training”.
Make sure third-party training is not allowed (no companies selected), then click Save.
To keep a video out of Google’s use entirely, the only option is not to upload it, or to delete it.
optOuts.effect: Keeping third-party training off means YouTube doesn’t authorise other AI companies to train on your videos. Google’s own training continues, and content already used stays in its models.

services.name: Zoom
services.summary: Zoom says it does not use your meeting audio, video, chat, screen sharing, files or other communications content, including AI Companion summaries and transcripts, to train its own or third-party AI models.

training.details: Zoom's terms of service and AI Companion documentation state that Zoom does not use any audio, video, chat, screen sharing, attachments or other communications-like customer content (such as poll results, whiteboards and reactions) to train Zoom's or third-party artificial intelligence models. Zoom treats AI-generated outputs such as meeting transcripts and summaries as part of that content. Feedback you choose to send about AI Companion, including the prompt you used, is used to improve the product but, according to Zoom, not for model training. The earlier AI Companion data-sharing option has been removed. The commitment covers communications content; it does not describe every use of service-generated usage data.

optOuts.title: Nothing to do: Zoom doesn't train AI on your meetings
optOuts.description: There is no training to opt out of. Account owners and admins can still limit which AI Companion features run.
steps: No action is needed.
Optional: account owners and admins can switch individual AI Companion features on or off in the Zoom web portal under Settings, AI Companion.
Avoid sending AI Companion feedback if you don't want your prompt shared with Zoom.
optOuts.effect: Zoom does not use your communications content for AI training either way. Turning AI Companion features off only stops those features processing your meetings.
